text:
She kept repeating to herself: “I have a lover! a lover!” delighting in the idea as though in that of another puberty that had come upon her. So at last she was going to possess those joys of love, that fever of happiness of which she had despaired. She was entering into something marvelous where everything would be passion, ecstasy, delirium; a bluish immensity surrounded her, the summits of feeling sparkled beneath her thoughts, and ordinary existence appeared only far away, down below, in the shadows, between those heights.

Then she remembered the heroines of the books she had read, and the lyrical legion of those adulterous women began singing in her memory with the voices of sisters that enchanted her. She herself was becoming like a real part of those imaginings and fulfilling the long daydream of her youth, seeing herself as that type of woman in love whom she had envied so much. Besides, Emma felt the satisfaction of revenge. Had she not suffered enough! But now she was triumphant, and love, so long held back, burst forth in its entirety with joyful seethings. She savored it without remorse, without anxiety, without uneasiness.

The following day passed in a new sweetness. They made vows to each other. She told him of her sorrows. Rodolphe interrupted her with his kisses; and, gazing at him through half-closed eyelids, she asked him to call her by her name again and to repeat that he loved her. It was in the forest, as on the previous day, beneath a clog-makers’ hut. Its walls were of straw and the roof came down so low that they had to remain bent over. They were sitting close against each other on a bed of dry leaves.

From that day on, they wrote to each other regularly every evening. Emma took her letter to the end of the garden, near the river, and placed it in a crack in the terrace. Rodolphe came to fetch it and put another there, which she always complained was too short.

One morning, when Charles had gone out before dawn, she was seized by the fancy to see Rodolphe that very instant. She could reach La Huchette quickly, stay there for an hour, and be back in Yonville while everyone was still asleep. The idea made her pant with longing, and she soon found herself in the middle of the meadow, where she walked with rapid steps without looking behind her.

Day was beginning to break. From a distance, Emma recognized her lover’s house, its two swallow-tailed weather vanes standing out black against the pale twilight.

Beyond the farmyard stood a main building that must be the château. She entered it as though the walls had parted of their own accord at her approach. A broad, straight staircase led up to a corridor. Emma turned the latch of a door, and suddenly, at the back of the room, she saw a man sleeping. It was Rodolphe. She gave a cry.

“There you are! There you are!” he kept saying. “How did you manage to come?... Ah! Your dress is wet!”

“I love you!” she replied, putting her arms around his neck.

This first act of daring having succeeded, now, whenever Charles went out early, Emma dressed quickly and crept down the steps leading to the water’s edge.

But when the cattle plank had been raised, she had to follow the walls running alongside the river; the bank was slippery, and to keep from falling she clung with one hand to clumps of withered wallflowers. Then she cut across plowed fields, where she sank in, stumbled, and entangled her thin boots. Her scarf, tied over her head, fluttered in the wind above the grasslands; she was afraid of the oxen and began to run; she arrived breathless, her cheeks rosy, her whole person giving off a fresh scent of sap, greenery, and open air. At that hour, Rodolphe was still asleep. It was like a spring morning entering his room.

The yellow curtains along the windows softly let through a heavy golden light. Emma groped her way, blinking, while the dewdrops hanging from the bands of her hair formed what looked like a halo of topazes all around her face. Laughing, Rodolphe drew her to him and clasped her to his heart.

Then she examined the room, opened the drawers of the furniture, combed her hair with his comb, and looked at herself in the shaving mirror. Often she even put between her teeth the stem of a large pipe that lay on the bedside table among some lemons and lumps of sugar, beside a carafe of water.

They needed a good quarter of an hour to say goodbye. Then Emma wept; she wished she never had to leave Rodolphe. Something stronger than herself drove her toward him, so much so that one day, seeing her arrive unexpectedly, he frowned like someone annoyed.

“What is the matter with you?” she said. “Are you suffering? Talk to me!”

At last, with a serious air, he declared that her visits were becoming reckless and that she was compromising herself.




X


Little by little, Rodolphe’s fears took hold of her. At first, love had intoxicated her, and she had thought of nothing beyond it. But now that he was indispensable to her life, she feared losing some part of it, or even that it might be disturbed. When she returned from his house, she cast anxious glances all around, watching every shape that passed along the horizon and every village dormer from which she might be seen. She listened to the footsteps, the shouts, the sound of the plows; and she stopped, paler and more trembling than the leaves of the poplars swaying above her head.

One morning, as she was returning in this way, she suddenly thought she could make out the long barrel of a rifle that seemed to be aimed at her. It protruded obliquely over the rim of a small barrel, half buried among the grass at the edge of a ditch. Emma, on the verge of fainting with terror, nevertheless went forward, and a man emerged from the barrel like those spring-loaded devils that leap up from the bottoms of boxes. He wore gaiters buckled up to his knees, his cap pulled down over his eyes; his lips were chattering and his nose was red. It was Captain Binet, lying in wait for wild ducks.
